projects.title: Mode/s of Making
projects.subtitle: Heat rotate cutting
projects.summary: I used rotary heat cutting to connect the shape of a polystyrene unit with the way it is made, then explored how those units could form an assembly.
projects.metadataDescription: A studio study connecting rotary heat cutting, custom polystyrene units, machine design and physical surface prototypes.
projects.context: National Cheng Kung University · Tainan, Taiwan
projects.role: Studio design research - computational design and fabrication workflow

sections.label: Context
sections.title: Begin with one unit.
paragraphs: Rotating the polystyrene blank changes how the cutter meets its surface. I explored this relationship as a way to develop custom units rather than treating fabrication as a final step.
The unit-geometry study provides the starting point: a shaped part that can be considered both as a cutting problem and as an element in a larger assembly.

media.caption: Original unit-geometry animation from the studio film materials.

sections.label: Profile to path
sections.title: Turn the unit into a cutting workflow.
paragraphs: I connected geometry development with cutting-path optimisation, G-code conversion and machine setup. The original workflow figure relates the layered unit and its cutting profile to these steps.
The unit model and the recorded workflow describe different parts of the same design process: what is being made, and how its geometry reaches the machine.

sections.label: Tool and blank
sections.title: Coordinate the tool and the rotating blank.
paragraphs: The machine study combines planar CoreXY-style tool movement with a rotating holder for the polystyrene blank. Motors, rods, belts and bearings coordinate tool and workpiece.

The original digital simulation shows the whole mechanism. The accompanying diagrams distinguish rotating and working areas and show the CoreXY motion frame; Arduino and Marlin provided control foundations for the workflow.

sections.label: Whole operation
sections.title: See the prototype make a cut.
paragraphs: The workshop recording moves from the digital mechanism to the built prototype. A mounted polystyrene workpiece rotates between its holders while the heated tool engages the surface.
This wider view keeps the blank, supports and cutter together. It establishes the operation before the next recording looks closely at the material contact.

sections.label: Material contact
sections.title: Look closer at the tool and material.
paragraphs: The studio film records the heated tip meeting the polystyrene as the cut develops. This closer view makes the material encounter visible at a different scale from the preceding prototype recording.

I connected the cutting profile and machine setup with material trials, using the resulting surface texture as part of the design study. The two recordings document physical cutting, not a simulated fabrication result.

sections.label: Assembly study
sections.title: Return from the cut to the assembly.
paragraphs: The opening assembly study can now be read through the unit, toolpath and physical cutting operation that informed it. I used custom units to explore how fabrication could shape an assembly design.

The image shown here is a digital assembly simulation from the studio film. The physical evidence on this page documents the cutting prototype and material trials; it does not establish a completed physical version of this assembly.

projects.title: Entrance Installation Art
projects.subtitle: Taichung Nan Shan no.6 Square
projects.summary: I helped turn a patterned entrance installation into coordinated 3D models and fabrication drawings within the PKD engineering team.
projects.metadataDescription: Scheme development, 3D modelling and fabrication-drawing coordination for the Taichung Nan Shan no.6 Square entrance installation.

sections.label: Context
sections.title: Develop the surface, then its openings.
paragraphs: I worked within the PKD team to develop an entrance installation from a continuous surface into individually defined folded panels.
The original study moves from a smooth surface through subdivision and panel depth to openings. Read these four states before comparing the alternative pattern schemes below.

projects.title: Dot-Based 3D Printing
projects.subtitle: Printing Architecture · Dot-based non-planar fabrication
projects.summary: I explored printing parameters and toolpath delays with Group1 to develop dotted surfaces across different geometries.
projects.metadataDescription: A 2023 ETH MAS DFab team project exploring dot-based non-planar printing through parameter samples, deposition strategies and physical prototypes.
projects.context: MAS DFab, ETH Zurich · Zurich, Switzerland
projects.role: Printing research - computational toolpaths and physical experimentation with Group1

hero.alt: A translucent twisted printed object stands in snow against grass and trees.
hero.caption: A physical prototype from the dot-based non-planar printing study.
hero.credit: Group1 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Namdev Talluru / JunJie.

sections.label: Context
sections.title: Parameters become material patterns.
paragraphs: I explored layer height, density, speed and pattern settings through printed samples with Group1. The surfaces reveal how those choices change bead spacing and texture.
We then carried the dotted surface language from small samples into curved and twisted geometries.

media.alt: A parameter diagram and twelve printed samples compare dotted and continuous textures.
media.caption: Layer height, density, pattern and speed are explored through a family of printed samples.
media.credit: Group1 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Namdev Talluru / JunJie.

sections.label: System
sections.title: Read the path through the deposited beads.
paragraphs: I worked on robotic paths and deposition delays with Group1. The original plate compares three path strategies alongside printed rings and close views of the deposited beads: read each row from movement diagram to material pattern.

The point model shows recorded low-speed path sample positions, not a finished solid or a complete fabrication sequence. The separate form study pairs printed shapes with line models to explore the strategy across different geometries.

media.alt: A translucent twisted printed object stands in snow against grass and trees.
media.caption: A physical prototype from the dot-based non-planar printing study.
media.credit: Group1 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Namdev Talluru / JunJie.

media.caption: Different deposition paths and time-delay strategies produce different bead patterns.

media.alt: Three printed shapes are paired with digital line models of their increasingly twisted geometries.
media.caption: The printing strategy is explored across a sequence of different overall forms.
media.credit: Group1 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Namdev Talluru / JunJie.

sections.label: Making
sections.title: Watch the pattern being deposited.
paragraphs: The original fabrication recording shows a nozzle depositing material along the specimen edge. It makes the relationship between movement, extrusion and the dotted pattern visible in a physical trial.
This recording, the sampled point path and the comparison plates are different kinds of evidence from our printing study; they are not presented as one continuous recorded operation.

sections.label: Results
sections.title: A family of physical experiments.
paragraphs: The physical prototypes carry the dotted surface study into different twists and overall shapes. They show a family of material experiments rather than a ranked set of optimal printing settings.
A translucent TPU prototype family extends the study into a lit display, where light reveals the bead structure and variation between surfaces.

projects.title: HC3DP Caustics
projects.subtitle: Inflation-based Pattern Exploration
projects.summary: With Group-Red, I explored how computational printing paths and inflated shells could produce different light patterns, moving between digital path studies and physical samples.
projects.metadataDescription: A Group-Red study of inflated printed shells, computational paths and photographed caustic light patterns.
projects.role: Computational design and fabrication research with Group-Red

hero.alt: A translucent printed form creates a radiating light pattern on a wall.
hero.caption: A photographed caustic pattern from the Group-Red experiments, not a measured optical-performance result.
hero.credit: Group-Red: Paul Jaeggi / Behnur Baiju / Kevin Seav / JosHsuan Chao.

sections.label: Shell and layers
sections.title: Begin with the shell and its layers.
paragraphs: I explored caustic patterns through simple shell geometries with Group-Red, drawing on Greek meander motifs and the Hilbert curve. The opening photograph shows a physical light experiment; the model introduces the patterned shell geometry.
The layer study below separates the bottom, middle and top point rows. Changes within each layer and planar layer addition provided the starting structure for the printing-path study.

media.alt: Transparent printed shells stand on a table, with light passing through their inflated surfaces.
media.caption: Physical shells from the Group-Red inflation and caustics study.
media.credit: Group-Red: Paul Jaeggi / Behnur Baiju / Kevin Seav / JosHsuan Chao.

media.alt: An original diagram pairs the printing tool and inflated shell with three parallel point rows.
media.caption: The original layer-slicing and curve-division diagram.
media.credit: Group-Red: Paul Jaeggi / Behnur Baiju / Kevin Seav / JosHsuan Chao.

sections.label: Points to frames
sections.title: Connect the points, then orient the tool.
paragraphs: I worked on the computational path study as part of the team. Connections between the bottom, middle and top point rows define the path in the first diagram below.
The second diagram adds tilted coordinate frames along that path. Read these as two parts of the computational workflow: where the tool travels, then how its orientation is arranged.

media.alt: Transparent printed shells stand on a table, with light passing through their inflated surfaces.
media.caption: Physical shells from the Group-Red inflation and caustics study.
media.credit: Group-Red: Paul Jaeggi / Behnur Baiju / Kevin Seav / JosHsuan Chao.

media.caption: The original diagram of connections between bottom, middle and top point rows.
media.credit: Group-Red: Paul Jaeggi / Behnur Baiju / Kevin Seav / JosHsuan Chao.

media.alt: An original diagram places tilted coordinate frames along a printing path.
media.caption: The original frame-arrangement diagram.
media.credit: Group-Red: Paul Jaeggi / Behnur Baiju / Kevin Seav / JosHsuan Chao.

sections.label: Path simulation
sections.title: Bring the path and tool together.
paragraphs: The original fabrication-path animation brings the tool, shell geometry and path frames together as a simulation of the printing strategy. It is not a recording of physical fabrication or a simulation of the resulting light pattern.
Our physical experiments were sensitive to air pressure and cooling. The digital path was therefore one part of the investigation, not a substitute for material trials.

media.alt: A printing-path simulation frame shows the tool and a row of red path frames.
media.caption: A still from the original fabrication-path animation; this is a simulation.
media.credit: Group-Red: Paul Jaeggi / Behnur Baiju / Kevin Seav / JosHsuan Chao.

sections.label: Samples and limits
sections.title: Read the samples and their limits.
paragraphs: The physical shells connect the path study back to the light experiment shown at the beginning. The photographs document observed forms and light patterns; they do not establish a quantified relation between a particular toolpath and optical performance.

Sticking and overinflation were also part of the investigation. The orange samples below show material departing from the intended shell geometry, keeping the process limitations alongside its visual results.

projects.title: Special Assemblies
projects.subtitle: V-Shape Modular Based Aggregation
projects.summary: I worked with Kevin Seav and Megi Sinani to explore reciprocal V-shaped stick modules and robotic assembly planning.
projects.metadataDescription: A 2023 ETH MAS DFab team study connecting V-shaped stick aggregation with robot trajectories and physical assembly prototypes.
projects.context: MAS DFab, ETH Zurich · Zurich, Switzerland
projects.role: Computational geometry and robotic-assembly research with Group6

hero.alt: A curved assembly of wooden sticks rises from a small base beside a robotic arm.
hero.caption: The assembled prototype beside the robotic arm, documented in the original Group6 record.
hero.credit: Group6 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Kevin Seav / Megi Sinani.

sections.label: Context
sections.title: A reciprocal starting point.
paragraphs: I explored V-shaped wooden-stick modules with Kevin Seav and Megi Sinani, drawing on reciprocal structures. Each addition changes the relationships between neighbouring sticks.
Physical prototypes connected this bottom-up geometric study with the conditions of robotic assembly.

media.alt: An early wooden-stick aggregation cantilevers from a small dome-shaped foundation.
media.caption: A physical study of the reciprocal stick aggregation and its foundation.
media.credit: Group6 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Kevin Seav / Megi Sinani.

sections.label: System
sections.title: Define a module, then its next neighbour.
paragraphs: I worked on the geometric aggregation study with Group6. The VStickModule diagram separates creating a V-shaped module from generating the next module using previous sticks. NE, NW, SE and SW choices organise directional growth.

The planning diagram then connects that geometry to robot trajectories: generate the assembly, plan through ROS/MoveIt, export JSON and inspect the simulation. Its failure-index branch supports replanning an identified trajectory rather than treating the first plan as final.

media.alt: A curved assembly of wooden sticks rises from a small base beside a robotic arm.
media.caption: The assembled prototype beside the robotic arm, documented in the original Group6 record.
media.credit: Group6 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Kevin Seav / Megi Sinani.

media.caption: The original VStickModule and directional-aggregation diagrams, with their figure captions.

media.alt: Workflow diagrams connect module generation, ROS and MoveIt planning, JSON data, simulation and replanning.
media.caption: The original software and JSON-based robotic planning workflow.
media.credit: Group6 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Kevin Seav / Megi Sinani. Project diagram.

sections.label: Making
sections.title: Inspect the planned robot movements.
paragraphs: The trajectory plate distinguishes pick, place, exit and insert movements around the growing structure. We studied stick ordering and tool-frame direction, including a Z-axis correction intended to reduce gripper interference with the table.

The moving source is a robot-assembly simulation, not footage of a completed physical assembly. Read it alongside the trajectory diagram; the original assembly model and the physical photographs provide separate views of the study.

media.caption: The recorded pick, place, exit and insert trajectory stages for V-stick aggregation.

sections.label: Results
sections.title: From modules to a prototype.
paragraphs: The front and top photographs show the physical prototype and the repeated contacts between its sticks. They bring the geometric relationships back to the material assembly.

These prototypes document the team’s physical exploration alongside the planning work. The photographs and simulation do not by themselves establish collision-free execution or a verified assembly sequence for every model part.

projects.title: Project Caschlatsch
projects.subtitle: Timber fabrication and AR assembly
projects.summary: I worked on computational design and XR production tools within the collective timber-tower project, connecting beam aggregation, digital fabrication and assembly.
projects.metadataDescription: Timber fabrication and AR-guided module assembly, with COMPAS XR feature development.
projects.role: Computational design and COMPAS XR development - ETH MAS DFab 2023-24 cohort project

hero.alt: Timber tower model on a stepped white site model in front of a window.
hero.caption: The architectural timber-tower model.
hero.credit: Source publication: Chia-Hsuan Chao / ETH MAS DFab 2023–24.

sections.label: Context
sections.title: A collective timber tower.
paragraphs: Project Caschlatsch brought the MAS DFab cohort together around a modular timber structure, connecting computational design, fabrication and assembly. The project developed at ETH Zurich and became a built installation at Disentis/Mustér.

We worked across a shared digital model, prefabricated timber modules and collaborative assembly. Within this collective project, my work connected computational design with the XR tools used during production.

media.alt: Timber tower seen through trees with visitors gathered at its base.
media.caption: The constructed timber tower on site.
media.credit: Source publication: Chia-Hsuan Chao / ETH MAS DFab 2023–24.

sections.label: System
sections.title: Connect indexed cells to timber modules.
paragraphs: I worked on the cohort’s voxel-to-beam aggregation in Python and Grasshopper. The five-class framework separates processing from geometry: ID manages indexing and neighbours, Discrete Vector Generator supplies directions, Voxel represents spatial cells, Beam the timber elements, and Layer groups of voxels.

A 26-direction discretisation defines candidate beam axes through voxel centres. Stored voxel data tracks existing beams to control intersections and avoid redundant crossings. The module plate then shows the material arrangement: an edge frame, orthogonal and diagonal supports, and five-beam or 30-beam infill.

My code work separated the aggregation solver and ID/vector tools for Grasshopper and refined occupied-voxel checks for the flying-beam problem. This was part of the shared research linking aggregation, module planning and fabrication; the original framework and infill plates below retain the detailed labels.

media.alt: Timber tower model on a stepped white site model in front of a window.

sections.title: Choose a module, then locate its beam.
paragraphs: During production, I improved COMPAS XR so users could select and switch modules from a cloud server, track beam IDs and follow the assembly sequence in real time. The original assembly plate follows these tasks through module selection, floating and orientation, module positioning and beam selection.

The annotated interfaces distinguish assembly and stacking tasks. Orientation arrows and a floating-beam view support component and cutting-feature inspection; scaling, three-axis rotation and stacking/assembly modes support module inspection and positioning.

Behind these tasks, a COMPAS Timber assembly plan supplies JSON building plans and checklists, with OBJ mesh geometry exchanged through Firebase to the AR applications. I also prepared Rhino-to-COMPAS data, converted stacking planes into frames and prepared module building-plan and mesh exports. My interface contributions sat within this collaborative CAD, cloud and XR system.

sections.label: Making
sections.title: One model, many hands.
paragraphs: The digital model connected beam geometry with fabrication and module assembly. Robotic and CNC processes prepared timber elements, while students worked together to assemble the modules.

The workshop brought digital planning into contact with physical handling and coordination. XR guidance was one part of that shared making process, alongside the people, tools and prefabricated components.

sections.label: Results
sections.title: From modules to a place.
paragraphs: The assembled modules create a route through the timber interior, with steps rising toward a lookout. Repeated beams form both the structure and the experience of moving through it.
The completed installation is a cohort and partner achievement. It brings computational aggregation, digital fabrication and collaborative assembly together in a place that can be entered and used.
